claims.text: Increasing chromium content in high-entropy alloys improves oxidation resistance.
The oxidation-resistance improvement from increased chromium occurs through formation of a protective Cr-rich oxide scale.
The baseline HEA may contain insufficient amounts of oxidation-resistant elements.
Increasing chromium during alloy synthesis is a method for improving oxidation resistance.
Aluminum or silicon additions may complement increased chromium in this alloy-design method.
Appropriate heat treatments should follow the compositional modification.
The method is intended for high-temperature oxidizing environments in which oxide-scale formation governs performance.
Increased chromium produces a continuous and adherent Cr2O3 or other chromium-based surface layer.
Chromium oxidizes preferentially upon oxygen exposure.
Preferential chromium oxidation forms a stable, protective oxide layer.
The chromium-rich oxide layer limits further oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Limiting oxygen ingress reduces the oxidation rate of the underlying alloy.
An HEA with increased chromium will show lower mass gain or a thinner oxide scale than an otherwise similar lower-chromium alloy under identical high-temperature conditions.
The lower-chromium baseline alloy has a higher oxidation rate and forms a less protective oxide.
The benefit of chromium depends on processing conditions and interactions with other alloying elements.
The benefit is limited to temperatures and environments in which chromium oxide remains stable.
The magnitude of the oxidation-resistance improvement and the effects of minor alloying elements are uncertain.
The proposed experiment varies chromium systematically while holding the other alloying elements and high-temperature exposure conditions constant.
Oxidation is evaluated using mass change, oxide-scale thickness, and oxide-layer composition.
The hypothesis is falsified if higher-chromium samples do not consistently show lower mass gain and thinner oxide scales than lower-chromium controls.
